Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Vignette:
Ethan Rourke was a 26-year-old detective who had come to treatment after months of trying to keep his life moving in the same orderly way it always had, even as something in him remained on guard. Before the trauma, he had built his days around work, his marriage, and the steady routines that came with being a police detective in a North American city. The assault he described had occurred in the apartment he shared with his romantic partner at the time, who had become physically abusive over the course of their relationship. Ethan spoke of one particular night in vivid, almost photographic detail: the argument, the sudden shift in tone, the smell of alcohol on the other person’s breath, and the sickening moment when he realized the situation was no longer merely tense but dangerous. He remembered feeling nauseous as the room spun with the force of the encounter, and he recalled the sounds that accompanied it with such clarity that, even now, fragments of them would sometimes force themselves into his mind uninvited. He said that when the memories came, they were not vague impressions but clear and detailed, as though he were back in the room, noticing the same angles of light, the same movements, the same sense of being trapped.

In the months that followed, Ethan found that the memory did not remain in the past in any orderly way. At times it would intrude without warning, and when it did, he sometimes heard pieces of what had been said during the frightening event echoing in his head. He described this as especially disturbing because the memories arrived fully formed, not as something he chose to revisit, but as something that forced its way into his mind when he wanted to be focused on work, his wife, or simply getting through the day. As a detective, he was accustomed to taking in difficult scenes, but he noticed that visible injuries or wounds on other people now caught him in a way they had not before. A cut hand, a bruised cheek, or an open wound on someone he interviewed could suddenly pull his attention and make him feel sharp, uneasy, and keyed in to what might be hidden beneath the surface. He also became acutely aware of the smell of alcohol. What might once have been incidental now had a powerful and immediate quality for him; if he caught it in a bar, at a social gathering, or on someone he encountered through work, he would tense and feel himself pulling back internally.

Over time, Ethan adjusted by narrowing his world in small but consequential ways. He avoided relaxing because it felt dangerous to let his guard down, as though the moment he settled would be the moment something could happen again. Even sitting quietly at home with his wife could make him uneasy if the evening felt too still. He had also come to numb his feelings rather than let them rise fully, describing this less as a conscious choice than as a habit he had fallen into because feeling too much made the memories feel closer. Physical contact had become another source of discomfort. He avoided being touched by others in almost any form, including casual contact that would previously have gone unnoticed. At work, he became more careful about stepping back from handshakes, pats on the shoulder, or the crowded proximity that came with interviews and scene work. The changes had not gone unnoticed by those closest to him, and although he remained functional in many respects, his marriage had been affected by the distance he maintained around touch and emotional closeness.

As he spoke about the trauma, Ethan’s language about other people had a hard, skeptical edge that seemed to have settled in after the assault. He said he had lost his faith in people, in life, and in any higher power he once believed might keep the world orderly. He felt like a permanent outsider now, as if whatever had happened had separated him from the ease other people seemed to have with trust. What frightened him most was the sense that people were not what they seemed. This was not limited to strangers; it extended into his daily work, where he was expected to read people carefully, and into his home, where he wanted to feel safe with his wife yet found himself watching for signs that anything could turn. That suspicion sat heavily alongside his efforts to function.

By the time he sought help, Ethan was no longer only trying to outlast the memories but was increasingly concerned by how much of his life had become organized around keeping them at a distance. He came in at the urging of his wife, after another evening when the smell of alcohol in a restaurant had left him visibly unsettled and withdrawn, and after he realized how often he was bracing himself against touch, rest, and stillness. He described wanting relief from the way the memory could seize him so completely, and he hoped treatment might help him feel less like an outsider in his own life. At the same time, he admitted that what he feared most was learning that he could not fully trust people again, even the ones closest to him.
